newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says N. Korea impasse no bar to aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says N. Korea impasse no bar to aid.

text.p: Despite an impasse in its Korean peninsula peace initiative, the United States on Tuesday pledged to continue providing food aid to North Korea and to continue a bilateral dialogue with its regime.
The pledges seemed an effort to underscore U.S. good faith even though the Stalinist regime in Pyongyang failed to unconditionally accept a U.S.-South Korean peace proposal.

"The North Koreans simply need to understand that we will come forward with our food aid no matter what happens in the four-party talks. They have not agreed to the four-party talks. The food aid is still coming," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"The North Koreans are just going to have to trust us and the international community that we mean well here," he said.

But he said the United States continued to oppose Pyongyang's demand for additional massive guarantees of food aid -- beyond $25 million in food aid recently promised -- before agreeing to join the peace talks.
Such differences "apparently will not be closed quickly ...The problem is getting a clear answer out of Pyongyang," he said.
After nearly a week of waiting around for North Korea's response to the proposal, South Korea's negotiating team flew home to Seoul Tuesday from New York.
U.S. officials remained optimistic peace talks eventually would be launched but were uncertain how long it would take.
At issue is a year-old U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing a fraying armistice with a formal peace treaty.
In addition to the United States, South Korea and its arch-rival North Korea, China would also participate.
At a meeting last Wednesday in New York, North Korea accepted the proposal in principle but conditioned acceptance on new food aid guarantees and lifting U.S. trade sanctions.

Despite several subsequent days of contacts between the U.S., South Korean and North Korean delegations and between the North Koreans and Pyongyang, the proposal's status remained inconclusive and the South Koreans flew home.

Still, the United States went forward Tuesday with a working level bilateral meeting in New York with North Korea on such issues as U.S. servicemen still missing from the 1950-53 Korean War, North Korean missile exports and establishing liaison offices in Washington and Pyongyang.
As with food aid, Washington does not intend to tie other issues, especially the fate of 8,100 Americans missing from the Korean War, to peace talks proposal, Burns said.
"We've got business to do (with North Korea) ... We're going to go forward and continue talking," he said.
U.S. officials told Reuters they did not have a good understanding of why Pyongyang failed to give a clear-cut answer on the peace proposal at the New York meeting.
"They need to sort things out on their side. I detect a little confusion in Pyongyang," one official told Reuters.
He said he believes the differences on the proposal can be bridged and will be bridged but when is hard to say.

If North Korea signals its readiness to finally reply on the proposal, the best tactic would be to convene another meeting of senior U.S., South Korean and North Korean negotiators but whether that would happen is undecided, U.S. officials said.
